content: 1. The decision to initiate treatment is not primarily driven by emotional or social support (ESS). Instead, high levels of treatment literacy and a clear understanding of the benefits of early treatment are essential. For example, one adult living with HIV in Zambia stated, “The doctor was clear. I knew treatment was hard, but the alternative was worse.” 2. While motivating people living with HIV (PLHIV) to start treatment may be relatively straightforward, maintaining long-term adherence to treatment is significantly more challenging. This is particularly true for specific groups such as pregnant women, children, adolescents, and key populations. Additionally, clients who felt pressured to start treatment or did not fully understand the lifelong implications and potential side effects often struggle with adherence. 3. Service providers noted that pregnant women are often highly motivated to start treatment to prevent transmission to their child. However, many default on treatment after delivery or breastfeeding. A service provider in Kenya explained, “Pregnant women are easy to initiate, but they often stop treatment after delivery.” 4. To ensure ongoing engagement in care and adherence, clients must have access to adequate and consistent supplies of free or affordable antiretroviral drugs (ARVs). However, in some countries, treating everyone is unrealistic due to resource and infrastructure limitations, raising questions about the feasibility of a “Test and Treat” approach. 5. Facilities must be easily accessible and offer services during hours convenient for clients. Limited service hours often increase the cost of treatment for clients, as they may need to make multiple trips to clinics to collect medications. 6. PLHIV frequently express frustration about the lack of perceived concern and support from providers, particularly regarding managing side effects. This lack of support can lead to treatment default. As one person who injects drugs (PWID) in Portugal stated, “If you feel worse taking medicines, you don’t see the point of continuing, and if you don’t know the advantages or how to manage them, it’s harder to understand why it’s important.” 7. Access to facilities with trained service providers who are sensitive to the needs of PLHIV and key populations is critical. Non-governmental organization (NGO) service providers are often seen as better equipped to provide quality services, including comprehensive support such as counseling and psychosocial services. 8. Provider and community adherence support is an essential but often overlooked component of treatment initiation and retention. This is particularly important for clients who start treatment while still feeling well. As one adult living with HIV in Kenya noted, “Support is critical to ensure those who start early stay on treatment over time.” 9. Facilities that actively promote adherence through counseling, pill counts, reminder tools, and mobile technology are effective in helping clients remain on treatment. Dedicated facilities for PLHIV and key populations are also valued for maintaining privacy and confidentiality. 10. National programs and facilities must address structural barriers to treatment initiation and retention, such as the cost of diagnostic tests, drug stock-outs, long waiting times, and limited clinic hours. These barriers often result in economic burdens, such as lost work time and multiple clinic visits, which disrupt care and treatment. 11. The terminology of “Test and Treat” versus “Test and Offer” elicited mixed reactions. Some felt that “Test and Treat” implied a lack of choice, coercion, or a focus on biomedical aspects without addressing psychosocial needs. Others believed that “Test and Offer” was too soft and might not encourage early treatment initiation. 12. Women, particularly pregnant women, often feel they have little control over the decision to start treatment. Many report that health professionals at antenatal clinics largely determine this decision. Within Option B+, some participants felt that women were not given the choice to discontinue treatment. 13. Women living with HIV are particularly concerned about confidentiality when starting treatment, fearing rejection, divorce, or violence. One woman in Ukraine shared, “It was difficult to accept that ART is forever, for all your life. It was difficult to make a decision.” 14. Key populations, such as sex workers, men who have sex with men (MSM), transgender individuals, and PWIDs, experience double stigma and discrimination. This includes stigma related to both their HIV status and their membership in marginalized groups. For example, a PWID in Ukraine reported, “Doctors just hate people on opioid substitution therapy and don’t even hide this.” 15. Specialized services and support tailored to the needs of key populations are essential. This includes training healthcare workers to respond to their needs, supporting standalone clinics for these groups, and investing in community systems to address social norms that negatively impact their health and rights. 16. Adolescents and young people living with HIV often feel excluded from decisions about their treatment. Many are put on treatment without being informed of their status or the purpose of the treatment, which creates significant barriers to adherence. One adolescent in Zimbabwe noted, “I didn’t know what I was taking or why, and this made it hard to stick to treatment.” 17. Supportive and sensitive healthcare providers, peer support, and shared experiences are critical for adolescents transitioning to adult services. However, many young people report a decline in the quality of care once they move from pediatric to adult clinics. 18. Parents and caregivers of children living with HIV often report that facilities are understaffed and not adequately trained to meet the needs of children. They also express fears about disclosing the child’s status, particularly regarding how the child contracted the virus. 19. Service providers face challenges in initiating and maintaining treatment among certain populations, such as children whose parents are not ready to accept treatment. Providers also note that pregnant women are easier to initiate on treatment but often struggle to continue after delivery. 20. Knowledge about viral load (VL) testing is high, but access to VL monitoring is limited in many countries, particularly in Africa and Asia. Misconceptions about VL results need to be addressed to improve understanding and adherence. 21. In Africa and Asia, VL monitoring is often associated with addressing suspected clinical failure, whereas in Europe, it is part of regular monitoring. Limited access to VL testing, high costs, and logistical challenges in rural areas constrain its effectiveness. 22. Parents and caregivers understand the importance of VL monitoring for their children’s health and treatment but report that most children have not been offered a VL test.
